title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning

paper.title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
paper.abstract: Abstract Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20–30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10–15%.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models perform well across a range of NLP tasks Yu et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) . However, achieving optimal performance in vertical domains such as medicine, law, and finance often requires instruction tuning on domain data, particularly for smaller scale models Ke et al. (2025) ; Slack and Al Moubayed (2025) ; Li et al. (2024c) . In practice, this process is subject to two budget constraints: domain data are abundant and unlabeled, and obtaining high-quality annotations requires costly expert knowledge; fine-tuning on all available data consumes substantial computational resources Xia et al. (2025) . Data selection provides an effective way to overcome these constraints: it can prioritize unlabeled samples to guide expert annotation and select the most valuable annotated samples for final fine-tuning. We therefore study how to construct an efficient training subset from a large unlabeled domain pool under joint constraints on annotation cost and computational resources. Top left: Four regional subsets are constructed by sampling 15% of the full training pool from each region. Darker blue indicates better performance on medical benchmarks after fine-tuning on the corresponding subset. Top middle: The best-performing region among the four, identified as the region containing high-value samples. Other panels: Distributions of samples selected by HC, Random, SPICE, and Coreset at the same 15% selection ratio. Existing data selection methods typically rely on labels to compute losses and gradients or assess samples’ influence on model utility Xia et al. (2024) ; Deb et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2025) ; Chang et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2024a) ; Yang et al. (2024) . However, this paradigm requires annotating the entire unlabeled pool in advance, making it difficult to satisfy practical budget constraints. Although pseudo-labeling allows these methods to be directly applied to unlabeled data acquisition, model-generated responses often contain domain-specific factual errors, which can introduce additional noise and distort the resulting selection signals. Meanwhile, though traditional active learning methods Sener and Savarese (2018) ; Ash et al. (2020) ; Ash et al. (2021) ; Kung et al. (2023) select unlabeled candidates using heuristic criteria such as diversity and uncertainty, these criteria characterize only properties of the data distribution and do not explicitly model candidates’ dynamic learning behavior during instruction tuning. Consequently, the key challenge is to accurately estimate a selection signal closely linked to downstream model utility before labels are available. To address this challenge, we adopt a training dynamics perspective to establish a selection signal that reflects the target model’s learning behavior. Building on Data Cartography Swayamdipta et al. (2020) , we monitor token-length-normalized response probabilities across training checkpoints to derive sample confidence and variability for instruction tuning (detailed in Section 3 ). As illustrated in Figure 1 , these metrics effectively isolate a high-utility data region that existing selection methods fail to target. While exact training dynamics provide an ideal selection criterion, computing them inherently requires ground-truth labels. To estimate this signal prior to annotation, we leverage prompt-only hidden representations extracted directly from the frozen target model. Prior research indicates that such hidden states intrinsically encode model-perceived difficulty Zhu et al. (2025) and semantic uncertainty Yin et al. (2026) . We hypothesize that these representations can reliably predict the target model’s training dynamics using only unlabeled inputs. Based on this insight, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework for data selection under both annotation and training constraints. The first stage, Progressive Candidate Expansion, addresses the annotation constraint. HC starts from a small expert-labeled seed set, extracting hidden-state features to train a proxy predicting confidence and variability. Due to limited initial labels, HC avoids a one-shot final data selection. Instead, it iteratively expands a candidate pool via active learning: the proxy scores unlabeled samples, experts annotate the top-K selections, and this newly labeled data refines the proxy for the next round. This process improves the recall of high-value samples within a limited annotation budget. The second stage, Exact Cartography Pruning, addresses the training cost constraint. Once the candidate pool is annotated, HC computes the exact confidence and variability within this smaller pool and applies a scoring function. HC then selects the final subset for instruction tuning from the candidate pool. This design connects the two stages: hidden states are used to cheaply recover a high-quality candidate pool from the unlabeled data, and exact cartography is used to precisely prune this pool into a much smaller training set. In this way, HC avoids relying on noisy pseudo-labels for full-pool selection while also avoiding the cost of annotating and training on the entire dataset. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formulate domain LLM data selection as a dual-constrained problem, where both expert annotation and LLM training computation are limited. We further identify LLM hidden states as a label-free signal for estimating sample training dynamics without relying on noisy pseudo-labels or full-dataset annotation. • We propose Hidden Cartographer, a two-stage framework with Progressive Candidate Expansion and Exact Cartography Pruning. The first stage uses a hidden-state proxy to recover high-value samples under limited annotation, while the second computes exact confidence-variability scores to select a training subset. • Experiments across medicine, law, and finance show that HC outperforms random selection and strong data selection baselines under the same budget. HC reduces expert annotation cost by 70–80% by annotating only a candidate pool, and training cost by 85–90% by fine-tuning on only 10–15% of the data.

sections.heading: 2.1 Data Selection for Instruction Tuning
sections.text: Data selection for instruction tuning uses signals such as quality, diversity, and model behavior Albalak et al. (2024) . Representative approaches include feature-based quality estimation Cao et al. (2024) , diversity-based selection with DPP Zhang et al. (2023) , task-aware distribution matching in TSDS Liu et al. (2024) , instruction-following difficulty (IFD) Li et al. (2024b) , information gain in FisherSFT Deb et al. (2025) , gradient-based influence in LESS Xia et al. (2024) , dynamic uncertainty in LEAD Lin et al. (2025) , uncertainty-aware self-reflection in SelectIT Liu et al. (2025) , gradient-conflict-aware selection in SPICE Chang et al. (2026) , weak-model IFD filtering with Superfilter Li et al. (2024a) , and small-model loss-trajectory clustering with S2L Yang et al. (2024) . These methods primarily select from existing instruction–response datasets, with many relying on response-conditioned signals, whereas HC guides expert annotation from an unlabeled pool and prunes the resulting candidates under separate annotation and final-training budgets.

sections.heading: 2.2 Active Learning for LLMs
sections.text: Active learning reduces annotation cost by selecting unlabeled samples using uncertainty, diversity, or both. Representative methods include uncertainty sampling, Coreset Sener and Savarese (2018) , BADGE Ash et al. (2020) , and AIT Kung et al. (2023) . These methods are effective when the acquisition objective is aligned with the downstream learning signal. However, for LLM instruction tuning, gradient-based acquisition is costly, and diversity or uncertainty may not reflect whether a sample is useful for improving the model. In particular, covering the representation space does not necessarily recover samples with favorable training dynamics. In contrast, our work uses LLM hidden states as a label-free proxy for dynamics-based sample value, enabling candidate expansion under limited expert annotation.

sections.heading: 4.2 HC Algorithm
sections.text: HC separates the process into two stages: Progressive Candidate Expansion, which uses limited annotation and hidden-state prediction to build a high-value candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and Exact Cartography Pruning, which applies exact training dynamics inside this candidate pool to select the final subset. The overall workflow is shown in Figure 2 . The first phase, Progressive Candidate Expansion, aims to reduce the annotation space by recovering a candidate pool with high coverage of valuable samples. The process begins with seed initialization, where HC uniformly samples a small subset 𝒮 0 \mathcal{S}_{0} from the unlabeled pool 𝒰 \mathcal{U} for expert annotation. This produces the initial labeled set ℒ 0 \mathcal{L}_{0} and initializes the candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , leaving the remaining samples in 𝒰 remain \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} . Because only samples in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} have target outputs, exact confidence and variability are initially computed exclusively within this small pool. Next, during proxy learning, HC tracks the output probability across training checkpoints for each annotated sample ( x i , y i ) ∈ 𝒞 (x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{C} to compute its confidence C i C_{i} and variability V i V_{i} . It simultaneously extracts the prompt-level hidden state 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} from the target LLM ℳ θ \mathcal{M}_{\theta} . The resulting tuples ( 𝐡 i , C i , V i ) (\mathbf{h}_{i},C_{i},V_{i}) are used to train a lightweight proxy f ϕ f_{\phi} that maps hidden states to training dynamics. Finally, HC applies this proxy to actively expand the pool. For each unlabeled sample x j ∈ 𝒰 remain x_{j}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} , it extracts the prompt-only hidden state 𝐡 j \mathbf{h}_{j} , predicts the dynamics ( C ^ j , V ^ j ) (\hat{C}_{j},\hat{V}_{j}) , and computes the corresponding selection score. The top-scoring batch is annotated by experts, merged into 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and removed from 𝒰 remain \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} . Repeating this cycle iteratively refines the proxy and expands the candidate pool toward the high-value region without requiring full annotation of the dataset. The second phase, Exact Cartography Pruning, focuses on reducing the final training cost. Although the candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is fully annotated after the first phase, it remains larger than the final fine-tuning budget. Furthermore, the initial scores are merely proxy estimates suited for candidate discovery rather than final selection. HC therefore recomputes the exact confidence and variability for every candidate sample using the target LLM and the newly available outputs. Because 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is significantly smaller than the original pool, this exact cartography can be performed at a manageable computational cost. HC then ranks all candidate samples by their exact training dynamics score, favoring learnable and informative samples while penalizing overly easy, unstable, or noisy outliers. The top N final N_{\mathrm{final}} samples are selected to form the final instruction-tuning set 𝒮 final \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{final}} . These two stages serve complementary roles. The first phase uses hidden states to allocate the limited expert annotation budget efficiently, distilling a large unlabeled pool into a dense candidate pool. The second phase applies exact cartography to prune this pool into a compact training set. Consequently, HC combines the efficiency of proxy prediction for candidate discovery with the precision of exact dynamics for final selection.

sections.heading: 6 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed HC framework. We first detail the experimental setup, followed by a comprehensive comparison with existing baselines, and finally present ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each core component. For a fair comparison, we include the cost required to compute HC’s training-dynamics scores in its reported training time cost. An analysis of the proxy’s predictive ability and the seed ratio selection are provided in Appendix C . The detailed adaptation of each baseline to the annotation-limited setting is provided in Appendix D.2 . The main paper reports LLaMA-2-7B results, while Qwen2-7B results and implementation details are provided in Appendix D.3 and D.4 . HC uses α = 0.50 \alpha=0.50 , β = 0.50 \beta=0.50 , and γ = 0.20 \gamma=0.20 as the default scoring parameters; all hidden states used in this work are extracted from the last transformer layer at the last non-padding token of the prompt; a detailed sensitivity analysis is provided in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate HC across three instruction-tuning domains: medicine, law, and finance. The training pools are constructed from corpora typically used by domain-specific LLMs Chen et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Yue et al. (2023) . For medicine, we use MedQA, MedQA-4, PubMedQA, MedMCQA, and MMLU-Medical Jin et al. (2020) ; Jin et al. (2019) ; Pal et al. (2022) ; Hendrycks et al. (2021) . For law, we select task-aligned objective benchmarks from the held-out legal pool: Exam, LED, and LCC. For finance, we evaluate on FPB Malo et al. (2014) , FiQA, and NWGI. All benchmarks use accuracy as the evaluation metric. Detailed dataset statistics, train-test splits, preprocessing rules, and task formats are provided in Appendix D.1 .

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: We compare HC with Full, Random, SPICE Chang et al. (2026) , Fisher Deb et al. (2025) , LESS Xia et al. (2024) , SelectIT Liu et al. (2025) , DPP Zhang et al. (2023) , TSDS Liu et al. (2024) , LEAD Lin et al. (2025) , Superfilter Li et al. (2024a) , S2L Yang et al. (2024) , Coreset Sener and Savarese (2018) , BADGE Ash et al. (2020) and AIT Kung et al. (2023) . All methods follow the same budget protocol in each domain, and label-dependent baselines are adapted with a two-stage protocol to match our unlabeled setting.

sections.heading: 6.2.2 Domin Experiments
sections.text: We compare HC against a diverse set of baselines under strict annotation and training constraints. Table 2 reports downstream performance across medical, legal, and financial domains. Overall, HC achieves the strongest average performance among budgeted selection methods in all three domains, while remaining competitive with or outperforming Full under much smaller training budgets. In the medical domain, HC obtains 51.54 ± \pm 0.16 average accuracy, significantly outperforming Random at 48.63 ± \pm 0.38 and approaching Full at 53.10. In the legal domain, HC achieves 44.65 ± \pm 0.60, substantially higher than Random at 35.43 ± \pm 0.27 and Full at 34.20. In the financial domain, HC reaches 77.86 ± \pm 0.66, clearly outperforming Random at 74.56 ± \pm 0.36 and Full at 58.64. These gains over Random are much larger than the corresponding standard deviations, showing that HC consistently improves over random selection across seeds. Across domains, label-dependent methods such as SPICE, Fisher, LESS, SelectIT, Superfilter and LEAD are often unstable under pseudo-label adaptation, while representation-based methods such as AIT, Coreset, and BADGE remain limited by generic diversity objectives. These results show that HC provides a more reliable acquisition signal under annotation and training-budget constraints. Figure 3 compares the runtime-performance trade-off in the medical domain. Representation-based methods are efficient but achieve limited accuracy, while label-dependent methods incur higher costs due to pseudo-labeling or gradient computation. HC achieves the best performance with moderate runtime, demonstrating a balance between selection quality and computational efficiency. Table 3 shows a post-hoc study comparing HC selected samples against human and LLM judgments of data value. The results demonstrate substantial agreement: the average O@10 across domains reaches 0.70 for a human expert, and 0.53, 0.60, and 0.60 for GPT-5.6, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and Grok 4.5, respectively (prompt details in Appendix D.5 ). sections.heading: Impact of stage 1
sections.text: We first study whether Progressive Candidate Expansion (PCE) can construct a high-quality candidate pool under the annotation budget. Replacing LLM hidden states with surface-level text features or sentence embeddings weakens candidate recovery under the same budget, showing that target-LLM hidden states better predict dynamics-based sample value. One-shot proxy selection is also weaker than progressive expansion, indicating that iterative refinement improves the proxy as more annotated samples are added. However, using more rounds brings limited gains while increasing retraining cost. Therefore, HC adopts 5 expansion rounds to balance quality and efficiency. Detailed results are reported in Appendix E.1 . We further replace PCE with existing candidate construction methods while keeping Exact Cartography Pruning fixed. As shown in the upper block of Table 4 , Random+ECP, SPICE+ECP, Coreset+ECP, and DPP+ECP all underperform HC. This confirms that ECP cannot fully compensate for a weak candidate pool, and that PCE is necessary for recovering high-value samples under limited annotation.

sections.heading: Impact of stage 2
sections.text: We next study the role of Exact Cartography Pruning (ECP). Table 4 includes two direct PCE variants: PCE (15%) directly selects a 15% subset in Phase 1 using proxy-predicted scores, without candidate expansion and pruning, while PCE (30%) uses the full 30% Phase-1 candidate pool for training without final pruning. PCE (15%) performs worse than HC, and PCE (30%) reaches similar accuracy but uses twice the training data. Other final selectors, including Random, SPICE, Coreset, and DPP, also underperform HC. This shows that ECP improves sample efficiency by pruning the expanded 30% candidate pool into an effective 15% subset using exact confidence-variability scores. The results for the financial and legal domains are provided in Appendix E.2 .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper presents HC, a novel data selection framework tailored for domain-specific LLM adaptation. Under strict budget constraints, HC leverages target-LLM hidden states to guide progressive candidate expansion, and applies exact cartography pruning to isolate a compact yet highly effective instruction-tuning subset. Extensive experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC consistently outperforms existing budgeted selection methods, achieving superior downstream performance while reducing annotation costs by up to 70–80% and training costs by up to 85–90%. Future work will explore extending HC to multimodal adaptation and reinforcement learning scenarios.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Due to computational constraints, our empirical evaluation is primarily conducted on 7B-scale models, which currently serve as the standard testbed in the instruction-tuning data selection literature. Although the core mechanisms of Hidden Cartographer are theoretically model-agnostic, verifying its selection efficiency on frontier-scale models requires massive distributed training infrastructure. Given that data selection yields more substantial absolute cost reductions as model size increases, a promising direction for future research is to apply HC to trillion-parameter architectures, potentially unlocking even greater computational savings for frontier model alignment.

sections.text: We provide a deterministic finite-pool analysis of the normalized, median-centered HC score. sections.heading: Appendix C Proxy Prediction of Confidence and Variability
sections.text: A central assumption of HC is that a small labeled seed is sufficient to train a proxy capable of accurately estimating the true training dynamics. To verify this, we train the HC proxy using prompt-only hidden states to predict the exact confidence ( C C ) and variability ( V V ). We then report the Pearson correlation coefficient ( r r ) on held-out examples as the labeled data ratio increases from 1% to 50%. Figure 4 demonstrates that the proxy effectively captures both training dynamics. Across the medical, legal, and financial domains, both correlations increase rapidly with a small number of labeled examples before saturating. With a 5% seed, the Pearson r r for C C and V V reaches approximately 0.79 0.79 and 0.68 0.68 in medicine, 0.79 0.79 and 0.68 0.68 in law, and 0.83 0.83 and 0.55 0.55 in finance, respectively. Increasing the seed from 1% to 5% yields substantial gains—particularly for the legal domain and for financial variability—whereas further expanding the seed to 30% or 50% produces only marginal improvements. This performance elbow at the 5% threshold justifies our seed size selection for Phase 1 of HC. Specifically, a 1%–3% seed underfits V V in the legal and financial domains, causing the subsequent active expansion to rely on an unreliable initial ranking. Conversely, increasing the seed to 10% or 15% yields negligible improvements in correlation while unnecessarily expending a significant portion of the annotation budget on random sampling rather than proxy-guided acquisition. Therefore, the 5% seed represents an optimal operating point: it ensures the proxy is sufficiently accurate to predict C C and V V , while preserving the majority of the Phase-1 budget for targeted expansion.

sections.heading: D.1 Dataset
sections.text: This subsection details how we construct the training and evaluation data for the medical, financial, and legal domains. All datasets are converted into a unified instruction-tuning format with three core fields: instruction , input , and output . The instruction field describes the task, the input field contains the question, context, or instance, and the output field stores the answer. For objective tasks, we additionally keep a choices field when candidate options are available, to enable evaluation via option scoring rather than unconstrained generation.

sections.heading: Medical domain.
sections.text: The medical training pool is constructed from MedQA ( Jin et al., 2020 ) , PubMedQA ( Jin et al., 2019 ) , and MedMCQA ( Pal et al., 2022 ) . For each source, we use its training split and randomly sample 20% of the records with seed 42. The sampled records are then converted into the unified SFT format and concatenated into a single training pool. MedQA and MedMCQA are formatted as multiple-choice medical exam questions, while PubMedQA is formatted as a biomedical yes/no/maybe question-answering task. The final medical training pool contains 80,852 samples, including 2,035 from MedQA, 42,253 from PubMedQA, and 36,564 from MedMCQA. For evaluation, we use five medical benchmarks: MedQA with five options, MedQA with four options, PubMedQA, MedMCQA, and MMLU-Medical ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . Their test sizes are 1,273, 1,273, 500, 4,183, and 945, respectively. Each benchmark uses a task-specific instruction consistent with its answer format.

sections.heading: Financial domain.
sections.text: The financial training pool is built from six FinGPT instruction-tuning datasets ( Yang et al., 2025 ) : sentiment classification, headline classification, financial relation extraction (FinRED), named entity recognition, FiQA question answering, and FinEval. We load the training split of each source, normalize every instance into the instruction / input / output schema, and sample 20% of each dataset with seed 42. This produces 41,032 training samples, including 15,354 sentiment samples, 16,432 headline samples, 5,511 FinRED samples, 102 NER samples, 3,422 FiQA-QA samples, and 211 FinEval samples. For evaluation, we use FPB ( Malo et al., 2014 ) , FiQA, and NWGI. The test sets contain 1,209 FPB samples, 239 FiQA samples, and 4,047 NWGI samples. All financial sentiment labels are mapped into the shared label space negative , neutral , positive . To avoid train-test leakage, we normalize the input text via lowercasing and whitespace normalization, and remove test examples whose normalized inputs overlap with the training pool.

sections.heading: Legal domain.
sections.text: The legal training pool is constructed from DISC-Law-SFT ( Yue et al., 2023 ) . Since the original dataset contains both objective and open-ended legal tasks, we filter it to keep only tasks aligned with our evaluation setting: legal examination questions ( exam ), legal event detection ( leg_eve_detec ), and legal case classification ( leg_case_cls ). Open-ended legal question answering and legal element extraction tasks are removed. For examination questions, we parse the answer into option labels such as A/B/C/D or comma-separated multi-answer labels, and remove explanation text from the target output. For event detection and case classification, we keep short label outputs and discard overly long generation-style targets. The resulting legal training pool contains 11,204 samples, including 2,908 examination samples, 4,198 legal event detection samples, and 4,098 legal case classification samples. The legal evaluation set is built as a task-aligned objective benchmark with 1,500 samples: 500 examination, 500 legal event detection, and 500 legal case classification examples. Training-overlapping examples are excluded when constructing the held-out legal benchmark.

sections.heading: D.2 Baseline Adaptation
sections.text: This subsection describes how we adapt existing data selection and active learning baselines to our annotation-limited setting. In their original formulations, many baselines assume that labels are already available for the entire training pool. This assumption is incompatible with our target scenario, where the initial domain pool is unlabeled and only a limited fraction of samples can be annotated by experts. Therefore, all baselines are evaluated under the same budget protocol as HC.

sections.heading: Budget protocol.
sections.text: For each domain, we employ a two-stage budget protocol. The first stage constructs an annotated candidate pool under the annotation budget, and the second stage selects the final training subset from this pool. In the medical and financial domains, the protocol constructs a 30% candidate pool followed by a 15% final training subset. In the legal domain, the protocol constructs a 20% candidate pool followed by a 10% final training subset. Thus, the second stage always selects exactly half of the annotated candidate pool. The same random seed is used across methods unless otherwise specified.

sections.heading: Full and Random.
sections.text: The Full baseline fine-tunes the model on the entire available training pool. It does not adhere to the training budget constraint and is included as an empirical upper bound. The Random baseline shuffles the training pool using the specified seed and directly selects a subset matching the final budget (i.e., 15% for medicine and finance, and 10% for law). Random selection does not rely on labels, model scores, hidden states, or training dynamics.

sections.heading: Label-dependent baselines.
sections.text: SPICE, Fisher, LESS, SelectIT, LEAD, Superfilter, S2L, and AIT Xia et al. (2024) ; Deb et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2025) ; Chang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2024a) ; Yang et al. (2024) ; Kung et al. (2023) require output-conditioned signals such as losses, gradients, influence scores, quality scores, response-loss trajectories, or response likelihoods under prompt perturbations. Since true labels are unavailable before annotation, we adapt these methods with a two-stage candidate-pool protocol. In Stage 1, each method operates on the unlabeled pool using pseudo-labels or pseudo-responses generated by the base LLM. The method then selects the first-stage candidate pool, which is treated as the subset sent to experts. In Stage 2, true outputs are revealed only inside this candidate pool, simulating expert annotation, and the same method selects the final subset from the annotated pool. For SPICE, the implementation first obtains pseudo-labels for each sample. If the input contains explicit candidate options, the pseudo-label is chosen by candidate log-likelihood scoring; otherwise, it is generated by the model. The method then constructs compact gradient proxies from the pseudo-label loss and selects examples using the SPICE Fisher/conflict criterion. In Stage 2, the gradients are recomputed using the true output of samples inside the expert pool. Fisher follows the same pseudo-label to true-label adaptation. Stage 1 builds pseudo-label gradient proxies and greedily selects samples by maximizing the log-determinant Fisher information gain. Stage 2 recomputes gradient proxies with true outputs inside the expert pool and applies the same Fisher selection rule. LESS is adapted by computing pseudo-label gradient features for the unlabeled pool and ranking samples by low-rank gradient similarity to a target gradient direction. When no external target set is specified, the implementation uses the mean training gradient as the target direction. In Stage 2, gradients inside the expert pool are recomputed with true outputs before final selection. SelectIT is adapted as a two-stage scoring baseline. In Stage 1, the model first generates a pseudo-response for each unlabeled sample. It then uses a reflection-style prompt to score the sample from 1 to K K and selects the highest-scoring examples as the candidate pool. In Stage 2, the pseudo-response is replaced by the true output, and SelectIT rescoring is applied within the expert pool. LEAD is implemented as a one-shot adaptation of its iterative data utility idea. Stage 1 uses pseudo-label losses to compute a static IDU-style utility score and constructs the candidate pool. The default implementation uses cluster-aware selection, where gradient proxies are clustered and selection quotas are allocated according to cluster utility. Stage 2 replaces pseudo-label losses with true-output losses inside the candidate pool and selects the final subset. Superfilter originally scores already-labeled instruction–response pairs with a frozen weak language model, using instruction-following difficulty IFD = PPL ⁡ ( y ∣ x ) / PPL ⁡ ( y ) \mathrm{IFD}=\mathrm{PPL}(y\mid x)/\mathrm{PPL}(y) and retaining examples with IFD < 1 \mathrm{IFD}<1 . In our setting, Stage 1 first generates a pseudo-response from the instruction and input with the target LLM, then scores that pair with a frozen GPT-2 (124M) scorer; the candidate pool is the highest-IFD subset among finite IFD < 1 \mathrm{IFD}<1 examples. Stage 2 reveals true outputs only inside this pool and recomputes IFD with the same frozen scorer. To match a hard training budget, if fewer than the required number of examples satisfy IFD < 1 \mathrm{IFD}<1 , we backfill from finite IFD ≥ 1 \mathrm{IFD}\geq 1 examples nearest the threshold; this backfill is an explicit budget adaptation of the original strict filter rather than a standard Superfilter practice. The weak scorer is never trained. S2L originally clusters examples by the loss trajectory of a small reference model trained on labeled responses. We keep that clustering rule, but Stage 1 trains the reference only on target-LLM pseudo-responses for the unlabeled pool. Each example is represented by its response-token mean cross-entropy at successive reference-model states (initialization, every 500 optimizer updates, and the final state). Selection uses Euclidean k k -means on these raw trajectories, with source-balanced uniform sampling inside clusters and a tiny-cluster fallback, matching the official implementation. Stage 2 reloads a fresh reference from the same initialization and retrains it only on the expert pool, using true outputs as labels, then repeats trajectory clustering to obtain the final subset. The default reference is Pythia-70M with full-parameter training; existing cartography fields ( C , V ) (C,V) and gold outputs are never used as Stage 1 features. AIT originally selects tasks by prompt uncertainty: the mean absolute change in the likelihood of a fixed response when instruction words are randomly dropped. We treat each SFT row as one selection unit and do not iterate model retraining. Stage 1 generates a pseudo-response with the frozen target LLM, then scores prompt uncertainty on that fixed response under 20 word-drop perturbations of the instruction (drop probability 0.2 0.2 ), keeping the input and answer template unchanged. Probability is the length-normalized geometric token probability exp ⁡ ( − NLL ¯ ) \exp(-\overline{\mathrm{NLL}}) on answer tokens, as in the official mean cross-entropy implementation. Stage 2 substitutes true outputs only inside the candidate pool and recomputes the same perturbation scores. Ranking is by prompt uncertainty in descending order. No scoring model is trained at selection time.

sections.heading: Representation and diversity baselines.
sections.text: Coreset, BADGE, DPP, and TSDS Sener and Savarese (2018) ; Ash et al. (2020) ; Zhang et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2024) are adapted as unlabeled or weakly label-dependent baselines. For these methods, the first-stage features are extracted only from the prompt side, i.e., the instruction and input, without using the gold output. The implementation caches target LLM hidden-state embeddings from the last prompt token and projects them to a lower-dimensional feature space. It also records entropy at the last prompt position as an uncertainty signal when needed. Coreset uses k k -center greedy selection over prompt hidden-state embeddings. In the two-stage setting, it first selects the candidate pool by maximizing feature coverage. In Stage 2, when true outputs are available inside the candidate pool, the method builds true-output gradient proxies and applies k k -center selection again within the annotated pool. BADGE uses an entropy-weighted k k -means++ procedure over hidden-state embeddings. The first center is selected by maximum entropy by default, and later centers are sampled according to a product of distance and uncertainty. This adapts BADGE to LLM instruction data without requiring full labels before annotation. In Stage 2, the method is rerun inside the candidate pool, using true-output losses as the uncertainty signal since expert labels are now available. DPP is implemented as a diversity-based unlabeled selection method. Each sample is represented by a normalized prompt hidden-state embedding, and selection is performed using a scalable pool-wise greedy log-determinant approximation. By default, DPP uses pure diversity without label-dependent quality weights. To match the two-stage budget protocol, we first select the candidate pool and then rerun DPP inside this pool to obtain the final subset. TSDS uses prompt hidden-state embeddings to estimate task-specific sampling probabilities. When no external query set is provided, the method samples a small self-query set from the candidate pool. It then assigns probability mass to nearest neighbors of the query examples and selects samples with the highest probability. As with DPP, TSDS is run once to construct the candidate pool and again within that pool to match the final training budget.

sections.heading: Fairness of adaptation.
sections.text: All adapted baselines use the same input pool, random seed, base model, and budget protocol within each domain. For label-dependent methods, true outputs are never used before the first-stage candidate pool is selected. They are only revealed inside the candidate pool to simulate expert annotation. For representation-based methods, prompt-side hidden states are extracted without using gold outputs. This ensures that all baselines operate under the same annotation constraint as HC.

sections.heading: D.3 Implementation Details
sections.text: All main experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU with 96GB of memory. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments use the same preprocessing pipeline, budget protocol, and evaluation scripts across methods within each domain.

sections.heading: LoRA fine-tuning.
sections.text: For all downstream fine-tuning experiments, we use AdamW with β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , ϵ = 1 × 10 − 5 \epsilon=1\times 10^{-5} , a learning rate of 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , a weight decay of 0.1, and an effective batch size of 64. Models are trained for 3 epochs with a cosine learning rate schedule and a 10% warmup. The final learning rate decays to 10% of the peak learning rate. LoRA uses rank r = 16 r=16 , a scaling factor of 32, a dropout of 0.05, and is applied to the attention and MLP projection modules. We use mixed precision and enable gradient checkpointing when needed for memory efficiency.

sections.heading: Training dynamics computation.
sections.text: To compute training dynamics, we train the target model for 5 epochs and save one LoRA checkpoint after each epoch. For each annotated sample, we evaluate the probability assigned to its gold output under every checkpoint. Confidence is computed as the mean gold-output probability across checkpoints, and variability is computed as the standard deviation. Both probability and loss are computed only over output tokens, while instruction and input tokens are masked out. Therefore, the dynamics reflect the model’s learning behavior on the target answer rather than prompt reconstruction.

sections.heading: HC proxy and candidate expansion.
sections.text: HC starts from a 5% randomly annotated seed set. The sample value proxy is trained on this seed set using hidden-state features extracted from the last token of the last transformer layer in the target LLM. The candidate pool is then expanded through active rounds, where each round adds another 5% of the training pool. For the medical and financial domains, HC constructs a 30% annotated candidate pool and selects the final 15% training subset. For the legal domain, HC uses a 20% candidate pool and selects the final 10% subset, following the smaller legal-domain budget used in the main experiments. After candidate expansion, HC recomputes exact confidence and variability within the annotated candidate pool and applies exact cartography pruning. The final score uses α = 0.50 \alpha=0.50 , β = 0.50 \beta=0.50 , and γ = 0.20 \gamma=0.20 to balance confidence, variability, and the extreme-sample penalty.

sections.heading: D.5 User Study Prompt
sections.text: This subsection provides the prompt used in the study involving human and LLM judges. For each domain, we randomly sample 100 candidate training examples and ask the evaluator to select the 10 most valuable samples for instruction tuning. You are evaluating data for private-domain LLM instruction tuning. You will receive 100 candidate training samples from the {domain} domain. Each sample contains an instruction, input, and output. Your task is to select the 10 samples that would be most valuable for fine-tuning a domain-specific LLM. Selection criteria: 1. Prefer samples that are domain-relevant and informative. 2. Prefer samples that teach useful domain knowledge, reasoning, or decision boundaries. 3. Avoid samples that are too trivial, noisy, redundant, or poorly formed. 4. Judge only sample quality for instruction tuning. Do not try to match any hidden algorithm. Return your answer as JSON only: { “selected_ids”: [id1, id2, …, id10], “brief_reason”: “one short sentence explaining the selection criteria” } Candidate samples:

sections.heading: Appendix F Sensitivity Analysis
sections.text: This section examines the effects of HC’s scoring parameters and the final training ratio on downstream performance.

sections.heading: F.1 Sensitivity to Scoring Parameters
sections.text: We evaluate how different combinations of α \alpha , β \beta , and γ \gamma affect the selected data region and downstream fine-tuning performance. To isolate the effect of the scoring function itself, this experiment uses exact cartography scores computed from labeled data, rather than proxy-predicted scores. All variants maintain a constant final training budget and employ identical fine-tuning configurations. We compare the following five parameter settings: (1) Equal C/V: α = 0.50 \alpha=0.50 , β = 0.50 \beta=0.50 , γ = 0.20 \gamma=0.20 ; (2) More Confidence: α = 0.60 \alpha=0.60 , β = 0.25 \beta=0.25 , γ = 0.15 \gamma=0.15 ; (3) More Variability: α = 0.30 \alpha=0.30 , β = 0.55 \beta=0.55 , γ = 0.15 \gamma=0.15 ; (4) Strong Penalty: α = 0.45 \alpha=0.45 , β = 0.35 \beta=0.35 , γ = 0.35 \gamma=0.35 ; (5) Weak Penalty: α = 0.45 \alpha=0.45 , β = 0.35 \beta=0.35 , γ = 0.05 \gamma=0.05 . Here, α \alpha controls the confidence term, β \beta controls the variability term, and γ \gamma controls the extreme-sample penalty. These settings test whether HC should emphasize learnability, uncertainty, or robustness to extreme samples. Figure 5: Sensitivity analysis of HC scoring parameters on the medical domain. The top row shows the selected regions under different scoring parameters in the confidence-variability space. Gray points denote the full training pool, and colored points denote the selected subset. The bottom row reports the corresponding average downstream performance. Figure 5 demonstrates that the Equal C/V setting achieves the best performance. The More Confidence setting concentrates selected samples in the high-confidence and near-zero-variability region, which primarily contains overly easy examples and yields suboptimal performance. Conversely, More Variability shifts the selection distribution toward highly unstable samples, similarly degrading performance. While Strong Penalty outperforms these two extreme settings by avoiding certain noisy or trivial regions, it still falls short of Equal C/V. Weak Penalty covers a broader region but proves less effective at filtering out extreme samples. Overall, these results indicate that high-value instruction-tuning data must strike a balance between learnability and informativeness while avoiding extreme regions. Consequently, HC adopts α = 0.50 \alpha=0.50 , β = 0.50 \beta=0.50 , and γ = 0.20 \gamma=0.20 as its default configuration.

Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. To address these limitations, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework that uses hidden states to guide annotation and exact training dynamics to select the final training subset. The first stage is Progressive Candidate Expansion, which utilizes the proxy to iteratively select top unlabeled candidates for expert annotation, merging them to recompute training dynamics and update the proxy until the annotation budget is exhausted; the second stage is Exact Cartography Pruning, which ranks these annotated candidates by their exact dynamics scores to isolate a compact subset under the final training budget. Experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC achieves the highest average accuracy among all budgeted baselines, requiring annotation for only 20–30% of the original pool and fine-tuning on just 10–15%. † † footnotetext: *Project leaders and Corresponding authors. Emails: sunyifan@ruc.edu.cn, zhaoxinf@buaa.edu.cn 1 Introduction Large language models perform well across a range of NLP tasks Yu et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) . However, achieving optimal performance in vertical domains such as medicine, law, and finance often requires instruction tuning on domain data, particularly for smaller scale models Ke et al. (2025) ; Slack and Al Moubayed (2025) ; Li et al. (2024c) . In practice, this process is subject to two budget constraints: domain data are abundant and unlabeled, and obtaining high-quality annotations requires costly expert knowledge; fine-tuning on all available data consumes substantial computational resources Xia et al. (2025) . Data selection provides an effective way to overcome these constraints: it can prioritize unlabeled samples to guide expert annotation and select the most valuable annotated samples for final fine-tuning. We therefore study how to construct an efficient training subset from a large unlabeled domain pool under joint constraints on annotation cost and computational resources. Existing data selection methods typically rely on labels to compute losses and gradients or assess samples’ influence on model utility Xia et al. (2024) ; Deb et al. (2025) ; Lin et al. (2025) ; Chang et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2024a) ; Yang et al. (2024) . However, this paradigm requires annotating the entire unlabeled pool in advance, making it difficult to satisfy practical budget constraints. Although pseudo-labeling allows these methods to be directly applied to unlabeled data acquisition, model-generated responses often contain domain-specific factual errors, which can introduce additional noise and distort the resulting selection signals. Meanwhile, though traditional active learning methods Sener and Savarese (2018) ; Ash et al. (2020) ; Ash et al. (2021) ; Kung et al. (2023) select unlabeled candidates using heuristic criteria such as diversity and uncertainty, these criteria characterize only properties of the data distribution and do not explicitly model candidates’ dynamic learning behavior during instruction tuning. Consequently, the key challenge is to accurately estimate a selection signal closely linked to downstream model utility before labels are available. To address this challenge, we adopt a training dynamics perspective to establish a selection signal that reflects the target model’s learning behavior. Building on Data Cartography Swayamdipta et al. (2020) , we monitor token-length-normalized response probabilities across training checkpoints to derive sample confidence and variability for instruction tuning (detailed in Section 3 ). As illustrated in Figure 1 , these metrics effectively isolate a high-utility data region that existing selection methods fail to target. While exact training dynamics provide an ideal selection criterion, computing them inherently requires ground-truth labels. To estimate this signal prior to annotation, we leverage prompt-only hidden representations extracted directly from the frozen target model. Prior research indicates that such hidden states intrinsically encode model-perceived difficulty Zhu et al. (2025) and semantic uncertainty Yin et al. (2026) . We hypothesize that these representations can reliably predict the target model’s training dynamics using only unlabeled inputs. Based on this insight, we propose Hidden Cartographer (HC), a two-stage framework for data selection under both annotation and training constraints. The first stage, Progressive Candidate Expansion, addresses the annotation constraint. HC starts from a small expert-labeled seed set, extracting hidden-state features to train a proxy predicting confidence and variability. Due to limited initial labels, HC avoids a one-shot final data selection. Instead, it iteratively expands a candidate pool via active learning: the proxy scores unlabeled samples, experts annotate the top-K selections, and this newly labeled data refines the proxy for the next round. This process improves the recall of high-value samples within a limited annotation budget. The second stage, Exact Cartography Pruning, addresses the training cost constraint. Once the candidate pool is annotated, HC computes the exact confidence and variability within this smaller pool and applies a scoring function. HC then selects the final subset for instruction tuning from the candidate pool. This design connects the two stages: hidden states are used to cheaply recover a high-quality candidate pool from the unlabeled data, and exact cartography is used to precisely prune this pool into a much smaller training set. In this way, HC avoids relying on noisy pseudo-labels for full-pool selection while also avoiding the cost of annotating and training on the entire dataset. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We formulate domain LLM data selection as a dual-constrained problem, where both expert annotation and LLM training computation are limited. We further identify LLM hidden states as a label-free signal for estimating sample training dynamics without relying on noisy pseudo-labels or full-dataset annotation. • We propose Hidden Cartographer, a two-stage framework with Progressive Candidate Expansion and Exact Cartography Pruning. The first stage uses a hidden-state proxy to recover high-value samples under limited annotation, while the second computes exact confidence-variability scores to select a training subset. • Experiments across medicine, law, and finance show that HC outperforms random selection and strong data selection baselines under the same budget. HC reduces expert annotation cost by 70–80% by annotating only a candidate pool, and training cost by 85–90% by fine-tuning on only 10–15% of the data. 2 Related Work 2.1 Data Selection for Instruction Tuning Data selection for instruction tuning uses signals such as quality, diversity, and model behavior Albalak et al. (2024) . Representative approaches include feature-based quality estimation Cao et al. (2024) , diversity-based selection with DPP Zhang et al. (2023) , task-aware distribution matching in TSDS Liu et al. (2024) , instruction-following difficulty (IFD) Li et al. (2024b) , information gain in FisherSFT Deb et al. (2025) , gradient-based influence in LESS Xia et al. (2024) , dynamic uncertainty in LEAD Lin et al. (2025) , uncertainty-aware self-reflection in SelectIT Liu et al. (2025) , gradient-conflict-aware selection in SPICE Chang et al. (2026) , weak-model IFD filtering with Superfilter Li et al. (2024a) , and small-model loss-trajectory clustering with S2L Yang et al. (2024) . These methods primarily select from existing instruction–response datasets, with many relying on response-conditioned signals, whereas HC guides expert annotation from an unlabeled pool and prunes the resulting candidates under separate annotation and final-training budgets. 2.2 Active Learning for LLMs Active learning reduces annotation cost by selecting unlabeled samples using uncertainty, diversity, or both. Representative methods include uncertainty sampling, Coreset Sener and Savarese (2018) , BADGE Ash et al. (2020) , and AIT Kung et al. (2023) . These methods are effective when the acquisition objective is aligned with the downstream learning signal. However, for LLM instruction tuning, gradient-based acquisition is costly, and diversity or uncertainty may not reflect whether a sample is useful for improving the model. In particular, covering the representation space does not necessarily recover samples with favorable training dynamics. In contrast, our work uses LLM hidden states as a label-free proxy for dynamics-based sample value, enabling candidate expansion under limited expert annotation. 3 Preliminary: Training Dynamics Score We use training dynamics to evaluate each instruction-tuning sample. In this section, we present HC, a two-stage framework for data selection under annotation and fine-tuning budgets. HC progressively selects samples from a large unlabeled pool for expert annotation, then prunes the annotated candidate pool into a subset for final fine-tuning. Direct optimization is impractical because evaluating selection strategies requires repeated annotation and fine-tuning. 4.2 HC Algorithm HC separates the process into two stages: Progressive Candidate Expansion, which uses limited annotation and hidden-state prediction to build a high-value candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and Exact Cartography Pruning, which applies exact training dynamics inside this candidate pool to select the final subset. The overall workflow is shown in Figure 2 . The first phase, Progressive Candidate Expansion, aims to reduce the annotation space by recovering a candidate pool with high coverage of valuable samples. The process begins with seed initialization, where HC uniformly samples a small subset 𝒮 0 \mathcal{S}_{0} from the unlabeled pool 𝒰 \mathcal{U} for expert annotation. This produces the initial labeled set ℒ 0 \mathcal{L}_{0} and initializes the candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , leaving the remaining samples in 𝒰 remain \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} . Because only samples in 𝒞 \mathcal{C} have target outputs, exact confidence and variability are initially computed exclusively within this small pool. Next, during proxy learning, HC tracks the output probability across training checkpoints for each annotated sample ( x i , y i ) ∈ 𝒞 (x_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{C} to compute its confidence C i C_{i} and variability V i V_{i} . It simultaneously extracts the prompt-level hidden state 𝐡 i \mathbf{h}_{i} from the target LLM ℳ θ \mathcal{M}_{\theta} . The resulting tuples ( 𝐡 i , C i , V i ) (\mathbf{h}_{i},C_{i},V_{i}) are used to train a lightweight proxy f ϕ f_{\phi} that maps hidden states to training dynamics. Finally, HC applies this proxy to actively expand the pool. For each unlabeled sample x j ∈ 𝒰 remain x_{j}\in\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} , it extracts the prompt-only hidden state 𝐡 j \mathbf{h}_{j} , predicts the dynamics ( C ^ j , V ^ j ) (\hat{C}_{j},\hat{V}_{j}) , and computes the corresponding selection score. The top-scoring batch is annotated by experts, merged into 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and removed from 𝒰 remain \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{remain}} . Repeating this cycle iteratively refines the proxy and expands the candidate pool toward the high-value region without requiring full annotation of the dataset. The second phase, Exact Cartography Pruning, focuses on reducing the final training cost. Although the candidate pool 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is fully annotated after the first phase, it remains larger than the final fine-tuning budget. Furthermore, the initial scores are merely proxy estimates suited for candidate discovery rather than final selection. HC therefore recomputes the exact confidence and variability for every candidate sample using the target LLM and the newly available outputs. Because 𝒞 \mathcal{C} is significantly smaller than the original pool, this exact cartography can be performed at a manageable computational cost. HC then ranks all candidate samples by their exact training dynamics score, favoring learnable and informative samples while penalizing overly easy, unstable, or noisy outliers. The top N final N_{\mathrm{final}} samples are selected to form the final instruction-tuning set 𝒮 final \mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{final}} . These two stages serve complementary roles. The first phase uses hidden states to allocate the limited expert annotation budget efficiently, distilling a large unlabeled pool into a dense candidate pool. The second phase applies exact cartography to prune this pool into a compact training set. Consequently, HC combines the efficiency of proxy prediction for candidate discovery with the precision of exact dynamics for final selection. 5 Theoretical Analysis In this section, we establish the theoretical properties of HC’s selection. We first detail the experimental setup, followed by a comprehensive comparison with existing baselines, and finally present ablation studies to analyze the contribution of each core component. The training pools are constructed from corpora typically used by domain-specific LLMs Chen et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Yue et al. (2023) . Impact of stage 1 We first study whether Progressive Candidate Expansion (PCE) can construct a high-quality candidate pool under the annotation budget. Replacing LLM hidden states with surface-level text features or sentence embeddings weakens candidate recovery under the same budget, showing that target-LLM hidden states better predict dynamics-based sample value. One-shot proxy selection is also weaker than progressive expansion, indicating that iterative refinement improves the proxy as more annotated samples are added. However, using more rounds brings limited gains while increasing retraining cost. Therefore, HC adopts 5 expansion rounds to balance quality and efficiency. Detailed results are reported in Appendix E.1 . We further replace PCE with existing candidate construction methods while keeping Exact Cartography Pruning fixed. As shown in the upper block of Table 4 , Random+ECP, SPICE+ECP, Coreset+ECP, and DPP+ECP all underperform HC. This confirms that ECP cannot fully compensate for a weak candidate pool, and that PCE is necessary for recovering high-value samples under limited annotation. Impact of stage 2 We next study the role of Exact Cartography Pruning (ECP). Table 4 includes two direct PCE variants: PCE (15%) directly selects a 15% subset in Phase 1 using proxy-predicted scores, without candidate expansion and pruning, while PCE (30%) uses the full 30% Phase-1 candidate pool for training without final pruning. PCE (15%) performs worse than HC, and PCE (30%) reaches similar accuracy but uses twice the training data. Other final selectors, including Random, SPICE, Coreset, and DPP, also underperform HC. This shows that ECP improves sample efficiency by pruning the expanded 30% candidate pool into an effective 15% subset using exact confidence-variability scores. The results for the financial and legal domains are provided in Appendix E.2 . 7 Conclusion This paper presents HC, a novel data selection framework tailored for domain-specific LLM adaptation. Under strict budget constraints, HC leverages target-LLM hidden states to guide progressive candidate expansion, and applies exact cartography pruning to isolate a compact yet highly effective instruction-tuning subset. Extensive experiments across the medical, legal, and financial domains demonstrate that HC consistently outperforms existing budgeted selection methods, achieving superior downstream performance while reducing annotation costs by up to 70–80% and training costs by up to 85–90%. Future work will explore extending HC to multimodal adaptation and reinforcement learning scenarios. Limitations Due to computational constraints, our empirical evaluation is primarily conducted on 7B-scale models, which currently serve as the standard testbed in the instruction-tuning data selection literature. Although the core mechanisms of Hidden Cartographer are theoretically model-agnostic, verifying its selection efficiency on frontier-scale models requires massive distributed training infrastructure. Given that data selection yields more substantial absolute cost reductions as model size increases, a promising direction for future research is to apply HC to trillion-parameter architectures, potentially unlocking even greater computational savings for frontier model alignment.
